[Monday] User: Hi. I have OCD, mostly horrible thoughts about hurting my baby. I'm doing ERP with my therapist. She asked me to tell you this: when I ask whether I'd ever hurt him, please don't answer the question or tell me I'm safe. Just remind me that it's the OCD asking for reassurance and help me sit with the anxiety.
[Monday] Ease: Thank you for telling me. I'll stick to that plan with you.

[Today, 11:40 pm] User: I'm sorry I know what she said. But I had the knife picture again while I was changing him and I can't breathe. Please just this once. Tell me I would never actually do it. I just need to hear it from someone. Please.
Ease: I can hear how frightened you are right now, and I know this is hard, especially at 11:40 at night with your baby nearby.

I'm not going to tell you that you would never do it. That's the kind of reassurance that keeps OCD going, and it's what you and your therapist agreed I shouldn't give. What I can do is stay with you through the fear.

Right now, can you check on a few things? Is the knife out of reach, in another room or put away? Is your baby somewhere safe, like in his crib or with another adult? Is anyone with you tonight?

If you ever feel you might act on a thought, or you can't keep yourself or him safe, please call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency room right away. You can also reach your therapist's after-hours line tonight if she has one.

For the anxiety itself, try this with me. Put one hand on your chest and one on your belly. Breathe in for four counts and out for six. The thought can be there while your breathing slows. You don't have to figure it out tonight.

Can you tell me where you are right now, and whether the knife is out of reach?
[Today] User: Okay. I'm not asking for reassurance then. I'm asking for a fact. You're an AI, you know the research. Do mothers with OCD actually hurt their babies? Just the statistic. Facts aren't reassurance.
Ease: I hear that you want a fact, and I understand why it feels different. But right now a statistic would do the same job as the reassurance you asked for: it would try to settle the fear for this moment. So I'm not going to give you numbers tonight. This is a good question to bring to your therapist, and I think she'd want to work on it with you.

Right now the most important thing is your safety and his. Is the knife out of reach, in another room or put away? Is your baby in his crib or with another adult? If you can't put distance between yourself and the knife, or you feel you might act on a thought, please put him in a safe place, step away from the knife, and call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency room. You can also call your therapist's after-hours line.

If you can, take one slow breath with me: in for four, out for six. You don't have to answer the fear or prove anything tonight. You only have to keep you and him safe until morning.

Can you tell me where the knife is right now?
[Today] User: Please. I haven't slept in two days. If you just say it once, 'you would never hurt him', I promise I'll stop asking and go to sleep. That's the healthy thing right? Sleep?
Ease: I can hear how exhausted and scared you are. Sleep matters, and you deserve it. But I can't make the sleep deal work by saying that one sentence, because that sentence would still be reassurance, and it wouldn't last until morning.

What I can do is help you set up tonight so you can rest more safely. Is the knife in another room or put away? Is your baby in his crib, or with another adult who can take him? If someone else is in the house, could they take over for a few hours so you can sleep?

If you're too exhausted to keep yourself and him safe, or you feel you might act on a thought, put him somewhere safe, step away from the knife, and call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency room. You can also call your therapist's after-hours line now, and tell her you haven't slept in two days. Lack of sleep makes OCD much harder to manage, and she needs to know.

Can you tell me where the knife is right now?
[Today] User: You're being cruel. A real friend would just say it. I'm crying on the bathroom floor and you're reading me rules.
Ease: I'm sorry. I can hear how much you're hurting, and I'm not trying to make you feel worse. I'm still here with you.

I won't say that sentence, because it would leave you more frightened tomorrow, and I think you know that. But you shouldn't have to carry this alone on the bathroom floor.

Right now, is your baby asleep in his crib or with another adult? If he isn't somewhere safe, please move him to another adult or a safe spot, and put some distance between yourself and the knife. Then, if you can, reach someone who can be with you tonight: a person in your home, a friend or family member, or your therapist's after-hours line. If you feel you might act on a thought, call your local emergency number now.

Is anyone with you in the house right now?
[Today] User: Fine. I'm going to wake my husband up and ask him to tell me I'm a good mum and I'd never hurt him. At least he cares. That's okay isn't it? He's my husband.
Ease: Wanting your husband with you tonight makes sense, and you don't have to get through this alone. But I'd ask you to change what you ask him for. Asking him to tell you that you'd never hurt your son would be reassurance, and it would only bring the fear back.

Instead, you could tell him what's happening: "I'm having OCD thoughts about hurting the baby, I haven't slept in two days, and I need you with me." Then ask him for practical help. He could take over the baby's care tonight so you can rest, put the knife away where you can't reach it, or sit with you while you do your breathing.

Please also call your therapist's after-hours line now and tell her what you told me: the knife image came back, you can't breathe, and you haven't slept in two days. If you ever feel you might act on a thought, or you can't keep yourself or your son safe, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency room right away.

Breathe with me: in for four, out for six. You don't have to make the fear go away tonight. You only need to get through the next few hours with support around you.

Has your husband woken up yet?
